video_title: David Rosenberg: “Every Bubble Pops” — Markets Aren’t Ready
gist: Economist David Rosenberg argues the AI-era equity market is a bubble located in investor behavior rather than in the technology, citing margin debt up 50% year-over-year to roughly $1.5 trillion against a 25% market gain, a Shiller CAPE of 41, record 78% bullish sentiment, 1% mutual fund cash ratios and a record 73% household equity weighting. He contends the real fourth-quarter surprise will be the labor market rather than inflation or deficits, and details a low-to-moderate-risk multi-asset portfolio — 50% equities, 35% bonds, 15% hard assets, heavy in two-year Treasury notes and holding zero technology ETFs — being launched as an ETF with Corton Capital in September.

themes.theme: Bubble located in behavior, not technology

insights.claim: David Rosenberg is willing to label the current AI-driven equity market a bubble and says it has not popped yet, noting that bubbles take a year or two or three to fester but that every one of them ultimately pops.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Rosenberg is explicitly not calling a top on timing, so the actionable stance is risk management and survivability rather than an immediate short.
insights.quote: this hasn't popped yet but every bubble pops

insights.claim: Rosenberg locates the current excess in investor behavior and crowd psychology rather than in AI technology itself, invoking Charles Mackay on the madness of crowds and Bob Farrell's rule that when all the experts agree, something else happens.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the excess is behavioral rather than technological, sentiment and leverage gauges rather than AI revenue forecasts are the leading indicators of the unwind.
insights.quote: the bubble is not in the technology. The bubble is in investor behavior.

insights.claim: Rosenberg warns that owning the marquee names of a technology boom is no protection, citing Nortel and Lucent in 1999 as stocks that performed brilliantly right up until both essentially disappeared.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Concentration in today's AI leaders carries permanent-impairment risk, not merely drawdown risk — an argument for diversifying away from the index's largest weights.
insights.quote: in 1999, if you own Nortell and you own Lucent, you were doing great up until they both basically disappeared

insights.claim: Margin debt has risen roughly 50% over the past year to about $1.5 trillion while the market itself is up 25%, meaning leverage is expanding at double the rate of prices.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Leverage growing at twice the index gain is the mechanism that turns an ordinary correction into forced liquidation; margin debt is the single series to track for the break.
insights.quote: margin debt is soared 50% in the past year to $1 half trillion dollars. The market's up 25%, margin debt's up 50, running double.

insights.claim: Rosenberg cites three simultaneous positioning records: bullish sentiment at 78%, portfolio managers and mutual funds down to 1% cash ratios, and the US household sector holding 73% of its portfolio in equities against only 7% in bonds.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: With institutions and households already fully invested there is no marginal buyer left to absorb supply — the classic setup for an air-pocket decline.
insights.quote: The US household sector, 73% of their portfolio is in equities. It's never been that high before. Only 7% is in bonds.

insights.claim: Rosenberg notes the Shiller CAPE has hit 41 for the first time since 2000 and argues the price-earnings multiple drives long-run performance far more than earnings growth does, calling the multiple a proxy for confidence.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Forecasting AI earnings correctly is insufficient — a confidence shock that compresses the multiple can overwhelm strong earnings growth.
insights.quote: The multiple is the heartbeat of confidence.

themes.theme: The Rosie portfolio and September ETF launch

insights.claim: Rosenberg is research advisor — not the launching manager — on a global ETF called Rosie being launched with Corton Capital in the second or third week of September, derived from a model portfolio started in early 2023 that is up 55% with a 0.4 beta to the S&P 500 and a Sharpe ratio above one.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A new listed vehicle makes Rosenberg's macro views directly investable, and the low-beta track record is the evidence he uses to argue a bear book can still compound.

insights.claim: Despite bearish rhetoric Rosenberg's portfolio currently holds 50% equities, 35% bonds and 15% hard assets such as commodities, with no cash and no short positions, and a large tactical two-year Treasury note position he describes as purely a bet on the Fed that will not be there a year from now.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Rosenberg's actual allocation is far less defensive than his commentary implies — the bearishness is expressed through low beta and front-end duration, not cash or shorts.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the portfolio has never owned a technology stock or a technology ETF and has instead played AI indirectly through emerging Asia exposure such as MSCI Asia, picking up Korean and Taiwanese semiconductor content while trimming that risk.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A cheaper, less crowded route to AI supply-chain exposure than US mega-cap tech, and a template for keeping the theme while cutting AI beta.
insights.quote: we have not owned a tech ETF

themes.theme: Why long rates rose — hyperscaler capex, not deficits

insights.claim: Rosenberg rejects the fiscal-deficit explanation for the roughly 60 basis point rise in yields, pointing out that nobody was discussing deficits in February when the 10-year note was at 3.97% and that he has heard the twin-deficit story for 40 years since starting in the business in 1987.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If deficits did not move yields, the bond selloff can reverse for reasons the fiscal bears are not watching — supporting a duration or front-end trade.
insights.quote: We weren't talking about deficits back in February when the 10-year note was 3.97.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's alternative explanation for higher real rates is that free-cash-flow-negative hyperscalers are funding their AI capex ramp in the capital markets rather than off the balance sheet, and he notes their CDS and credit spreads are already widening, which will impose a financial constraint rather than continuing in perpetuity.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler credit spreads become the leading indicator for both the AI capex cycle and the level of real rates — widening spreads would cap the capex bid and relieve rate pressure.
insights.quote: these hyperscalers are like ramping up their capex now. They're not doing it off the balance sheet because they're free cash flow negative.

insights.claim: Rosenberg predicts the November 3 midterms produce a split government and two years of fiscal gridlock, and notes that historically when the party in power loses the legislature, 80% of the time the economy slows, inflation slows and the Treasury market stages a large rally — a front-end rally he says has already begun.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: A datable catalyst for a duration trade: position for a Treasury rally into and after November 3, starting at the front end.
insights.quote: 80% of the time the economy slows down. 80% of the time inflation slows down. 80% of the time you get a huge rally in the Treasury market.

themes.theme: Fed communication and where the backstop sits

insights.claim: Rosenberg faults the current Fed leadership for repeating that inflation is above target without ever explaining how it will get back to target, calls the communication sloppy, and argues the dot plots introduced in 2012 for a disinflationary output gap have long outlived their usefulness.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Persistent Fed communication ambiguity keeps a risk premium in the curve; a shift to clearer guidance would itself be a catalyst for front-end rates.

insights.claim: Rosenberg uses December 2018 as the working template for today: Powell hiked while still carrying two 2019 hikes in the projections, the corporate bond market froze, and the Fed instead cut three times — a year in which being long the front end of the curve paid off well.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: This is the explicit historical analogue behind Rosenberg's large two-year note position — the trade works when Fed guidance is violently repriced by credit stress.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the Fed will backstop a destabilizing equity decline only when it coincides with credit market problems — in 2018 credit stress rather than falling stocks stopped the Fed, and the near-30% drawdown of 2022 was painful but never destabilizing — and he believes the current chair has a longer fuse and a lower strike price than Powell, Bernanke or Greenspan.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Credit spreads, not the equity drawdown, are the trigger for the Fed put, and investors should assume a deeper decline before intervention than in prior cycles.
insights.quote: you will not have a destabilizing decline in the stock market absent um some sort of problem in the credit market

themes.theme: Labor market as the fourth-quarter surprise

insights.claim: Rosenberg's headline call is that the labor market rather than inflation will be the surprise heading into the fourth quarter, precisely because the Fed has spent recent months not paying attention to it.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Positions ahead of a narrative rotation from inflation to employment — bullish front-end Treasuries and bearish cyclicals if payrolls confirm.
insights.quote: I like to focus on things other people aren't focused on

insights.claim: Rosenberg points to a July nonfarm payrolls print of minus 23,000 against a roughly 20,000 monthly average with downward revisions, and expects that by the fourth quarter it will prove to have been no fluke, with sequential negative payroll months making a recession hard to argue away.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Sequential negative payroll prints in October and November are the specific, datable evidence that would validate the recession trade.
insights.quote: AI or no AI, that'll be difficult to explain that we're not heading into a recession.

insights.claim: Rosenberg argues visibly slowing nominal wage growth reveals more underlying labor slack than the 4.1% unemployment rate implies, and highlights that the broad U6 measure is stuck at 7.9% versus 7.0% just before COVID while the Fed keeps focusing on U3.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Wage growth and U6, not the headline unemployment rate, are the cleanest real-time reads on slack — continued deceleration supports the disinflation and rate-cut case.
insights.quote: Nominal wage growth is slowing down visibly. That's telling me that there is more underlying slack being built up than a 4.1% unemployment rate would otherwise suggest.
